auditMetadata.systemName: Sentinal Digital Operations Hub & CTF Wars Platform

findings.title: Client-Side Token Eviction and Permanent Dashboard Infinite Loading Trap
findings.symptom: Direct navigation or browser reload on any /dashboard/* route triggers an unresolvable infinite spinner ('Initializing Operative Interface...' or 'Loading Analytics Engine...').
findings.rootCause: The Express backend sets the accessToken cookie with HttpOnly: true. During client-side bootstrap, AuthContext executes fetchMe() which calls Cookies.get('accessToken'). Because js-cookie cannot read HttpOnly cookies, it returns undefined, resetting in-memory token state to an empty string. The dashboard routes guard data-fetching with 'if (!token || !user) return;'. Consequently, data fetching never executes and loading state initialized to true is never flipped to false.
reproductionSteps: 1. Authenticate at http://localhost:3000/auth using valid credentials.
2. Observe redirection to http://localhost:3000/dashboard.
3. Press F5 (Page Refresh) or enter http://localhost:3000/dashboard/analytics directly in the address bar.
4. Observe indefinite loading screen with zero network requests dispatched.
findings.remediation: Standardize authentication state handling. Either provide an authenticated /api/auth/me session handshake endpoint that verifies the HttpOnly cookie and returns user context without requiring client-accessible token strings, or adjust cookie accessibility if non-HttpOnly tokens are required by client architecture.

findings.title: Unhandled Redis Promise Rejection Terminating CTF Backend Process on User Interaction
findings.symptom: Clicking any challenge card or emitting a 'viewChallenge' WebSocket event crashes the CTF backend server process (Node.js PID terminates with exit code 1), dropping all live connections.
findings.rootCause: In scoreboard.ts line 42, 'await redis.sadd(presenceKey, socket.id)' is invoked without verifying whether the Redis client is connected. When Redis is inactive, ioredis rejects the command with 'Error: Connection is closed.'. Because this rejection is not caught within a try-catch block, Node.js triggers an unhandled promise rejection that terminates the process.
reproductionSteps: 1. Ensure Redis service on port 6379 is offline.
2. Start CTF server via npm run dev on port 5001.
3. Connect to http://localhost:3001/challenges.
4. Click on any challenge card to view details.
5. Observe immediate crash of node process on port 5001 with 'Error: Connection is closed.'.
findings.remediation: Wrap all Redis operations in availability guards: check redis.status === 'ready' before dispatching commands, and wrap calls in try-catch blocks with graceful degradation to in-memory fallback state.

findings.title: Horizontal Viewport Overflow on Mobile Displays Below 345px Width
findings.symptom: On screen widths of 320px (e.g. iPhone SE / narrow mobile), the horizontal layout overflows by 21px (bounding box right coordinate: 341px), pushing navigation buttons off-screen and introducing unintended horizontal scroll.
findings.rootCause: In Navbar.tsx, the header container combines the logo component (~176px), action button (~90px), mobile menu trigger (~36px), flexbox gaps (gap-3 = 12px), and container padding (px-4 = 32px), creating an irreducible minimum width of 346px.
reproductionSteps: 1. Open http://localhost:3000 in browser.
2. Set viewport dimensions to 320px × 568px.
3. Observe horizontal scrollbar appearing.
4. Inspect navigation element right boundary: 341.2px > 320px.
findings.remediation: Introduce responsive container queries or mobile breakpoint adjustments: hide secondary header buttons on viewports below 360px, reduce logo text sizing, or reduce container padding to px-2 on narrow displays.

findings.title: Misleading Empty State on Challenge Board for Unregistered Users
findings.symptom: Navigating to http://localhost:3001/challenges without having previously joined the competition displays '0 challenges available / No challenges available yet.' with no error or call-to-action.
findings.rootCause: The API endpoint GET /api/challenges returns HTTP 400 with { success: false, message: 'You must join this competition first.' }. The frontend component fails to evaluate the success flag or error message, sets loading to false, and defaults to the empty state view.
reproductionSteps: 1. Sign in to CTF platform with an account that has not joined Operation Hikari.
2. Navigate directly to http://localhost:3001/challenges.
3. Observe empty board with '0 challenges available'.
findings.remediation: Handle the specific error response by rendering an actionable modal or banner prompting the user to enter the competition invite code, or automatically redirecting to the competition lobby.

findings.title: HTTP Status 429 Misused for Incorrect CTF Flag Guesses
findings.symptom: Submitting an incorrect flag to POST /api/submissions returns HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests instead of a 200 OK result or 400 Bad Request.
findings.rootCause: In submissions.ts line 203, failed flag validation executes res.status(429).json({ success: false, message: 'Incorrect flag. Try again.' }). This violates RFC 6585, confusing reverse proxies, API gateways, and client error handlers into triggering rate-limiting backoff algorithms.
reproductionSteps: 1. Submit an invalid flag string to POST http://localhost:5001/api/submissions.
2. Inspect HTTP response status code.
3. Observe HTTP status 429 returned for a single initial attempt.
findings.remediation: Return HTTP 200 with { success: false, correct: false, message: 'Incorrect flag.' } or HTTP 400, reserving HTTP 429 strictly for actual rate-limit threshold exhaustion.

findings.title: Missing ARIA Labels on Interactive Icon Buttons
findings.symptom: Screen readers announce 'button' with no name or purpose on critical controls including password visibility toggle, mobile menu button, and all CTF sidebar links.
findings.rootCause: Buttons wrap raw SVG icons without aria-label, aria-labelledby, or visually-hidden accessible text elements.
reproductionSteps: 1. Inspect password visibility toggle button on http://localhost:3000/auth.
2. Inspect mobile hamburger button in Navbar.
3. Inspect sidebar navigation icons in CTF AppShell.
4. Confirm aria-label is null on all elements.
findings.remediation: Add explicit aria-label attributes (e.g., aria-label='Toggle password visibility', aria-label='Open navigation menu', aria-label='Scoreboard') to all icon-only button elements.

findings.title: Heading Hierarchy Level Skipping on Landing Page
findings.symptom: Document structure skips from H2 directly to H4 under the Defense Pillars section, violating WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.3.1.
findings.rootCause: PillarsSection utilizes <h4> tags for pillar card titles immediately underneath the section's <h2> header, omitting the structural <h3> level.
reproductionSteps: 1. Inspect DOM of http://localhost:3000.

2. Locate section title:

DEFENSE PILLARS

.

3. Locate immediately nested pillar titles:

CYBER DEFENSE

, omitting

.
findings.remediation: Change card titles from <h4> to <h3>, maintaining sequential heading hierarchy.

findings.title: Hardcoded Unicode Emoji Literals in Event Match Routing Logic
findings.symptom: Source code contains hardcoded unicode emoji literals in string comparisons and badge renderers, violating workspace zero-emoji standard.
findings.rootCause: In events/page.tsx lines 30-37, logic contains emoji characters (camera, speech bubble, etc.) for event category mapping.
reproductionSteps: 1. Inspect client/src/app/dashboard/events/page.tsx lines 30-37.
2. Observe emoji literal characters embedded in code.
findings.remediation: Replace emoji literals with typed enums, Lucide icons, or structured symbols.

findings.title: Development JIT Compilation Latency Spikes on Route Traversal
findings.symptom: First navigation to cold dashboard routes results in TTFB of 500ms to 940ms under Next.js dev server.
findings.rootCause: Next.js on-demand compilation in development mode recompiles TSX trees and CSS bundles upon first route hit.
reproductionSteps: 1. Trigger cold hit on /team or /about.
2. Inspect duration in http_route_probe.json: /team = 940ms, /about = 654ms.
findings.remediation: Execute production build (next build) for performance benchmarking and production deployment to enable pre-rendered static assets and cached route segments.

findings.title: High Memory Footprint Across Dual Next.js Development Instances
findings.symptom: Simultaneously running two Next.js dev instances consumes 3.44 GB commit charge across Node.js processes.
findings.rootCause: Next.js dev server maintains persistent AST caches, SWC compiler instances, and in-memory Webpack/Turbopack graphs for both frontend codebases.
reproductionSteps: 1. Inspect OS process manager with both frontends running.
2. Observe Node.js memory allocations totaling ~3.44 GB.
findings.remediation: Consolidate into a unified Next.js multi-zone or turborepo workspace, or run production bundles locally during extended multi-service testing.
